workload.problem: damped harmonic oscillator x'' + 2 zeta omega x' + omega^2 x = 0, classical RK4, fixed step

arms.eagle_graph_steps: eagle graph, K fused steps per launch
arms.eagle_graph_steps_compact: eagle graph, K fused steps per launch + compaction
arms.eagle_graph_auto: eagle auto (eagle picks the launch mode)

arms.eagle_graph: The step written once as a hawk kernel; the whole loop runs on the device as one CUDA graph with a device-side stop guard, so a run is one launch with no host round trip per step. On this card: N = 1,000,000, spread S=100: 10.3 ms; spread S=1000: 94.4 ms; uniform S=1000: 105 ms. Fastest in 0 of 12 cells.
arms.eagle_graph_compact: Adds an active-set map: the launch covers only the samples still running, rebuilt every 16 steps; it is made for batches that thin out (the spread configurations). On this card: N = 1,000,000, spread S=100: 5.45 ms (0.527× the eagle graph time); spread S=1000: 39.3 ms (0.417× the eagle graph time); uniform S=1000: 133 ms (1.27× the eagle graph time). Fastest in 0 of 12 cells.
arms.eagle_graph_reorder: Adds a physical reorder when the live samples spread thin over their warps, so the mapped reads stay contiguous; the final restore to sample order is inside its wall. On this card: N = 1,000,000, spread S=100: 6.73 ms (0.651× the eagle graph time); spread S=1000: 39.3 ms (0.417× the eagle graph time); uniform S=1000: 134 ms (1.27× the eagle graph time). Fastest in 0 of 12 cells.
arms.eagle_graph_steps: The same step with one decorator argument, @hawk.kernel(steps=16): each launch runs that many steps per sample with the state kept in registers, as Warp's per-thread loop does, and the launches, guard checks and plane reads shrink by the same factor; its results are bit-identical to the eagle graph arm's in every cell. K is chosen by hand here; the eagle_graph_auto arm picks it at run time. On this card: N = 1,000,000, spread S=100: 9.77 ms (0.945× the eagle graph time); spread S=1000: 93.9 ms (0.994× the eagle graph time); uniform S=1000: 106 ms (1.01× the eagle graph time). Fastest in 0 of 12 cells.
arms.eagle_graph_steps_compact: The K-steps kernel over the active-set map: the register-resident steps of the arm above, and the launches cover only the samples still running, so it fits batches that thin out. On this card: N = 1,000,000, spread S=100: 7.6 ms (0.735× the eagle graph time); spread S=1000: 28.5 ms (0.302× the eagle graph time); uniform S=1000: 106 ms (1.01× the eagle graph time). Fastest in 0 of 12 cells.
arms.eagle_graph_auto: The same step with @hawk.kernel(steps="auto") on the active-set kind, and nothing to tune: it picks the steps per launch itself after every launch, on the device, so a batch whose samples all run to the end gets Warp-like fusion of up to 64 steps per launch, and a batch that thins out gets shorter launches with the active set compacted after each one; no sample takes more steps than the cap. On this card: N = 1,000,000, spread S=100: 4.71 ms (0.456× the eagle graph time); spread S=1000: 25.3 ms (0.268× the eagle graph time); uniform S=1000: 103 ms (0.979× the eagle graph time). Fastest in 11 of 12 cells.
arms.eagle_graph_persist: The plain (not active-set) automatic kernel, forced through hawk's persist entry: one launch, no graph, no map, no policy kernel, no cap at 64 -- a grid of SMs blocks of 256 lanes each steal the next unfinished sample off a counter when their own finishes, so idle warps refill without ever rebuilding an index map; made for batches too large for one resident wave. On this card: N = 1,000,000, spread S=100: 4.76 ms (0.46× the eagle graph time); spread S=1000: 25.4 ms (0.269× the eagle graph time); uniform S=1000: 103 ms (0.98× the eagle graph time). Fastest in 0 of 12 cells.
arms.eagle_simulate: The same automatic kernel through eagle.simulate: the model, its state and its parameters by name, with no plan or plane binding to write; eagle deploys the kernel and builds the same device loop. On this card: N = 1,000,000, spread S=100: 4.73 ms (0.457× the eagle graph time); spread S=1000: 25.3 ms (0.269× the eagle graph time); uniform S=1000: 103 ms (0.979× the eagle graph time). Fastest in 1 of 12 cells.
arms.eager_loop: The same kernels launched from Python one step at a time; the host sees the state after every step. On this card: N = 1,000,000, spread S=100: 14.5 ms (1.4× the eagle graph time); spread S=1000: 146 ms (1.54× the eagle graph time); uniform S=1000: 158 ms (1.5× the eagle graph time). Fastest in 0 of 12 cells.
arms.cupy_masked: NumPy-like array code on GPUs with no kernel to write; every sample is computed every step, so it fits dense batches where all samples run to the end (the uniform configuration). On this card: N = 1,000,000, spread S=100: 159 ms (15.4× the eagle graph time); spread S=1000: 1.6 s (17× the eagle graph time); uniform S=1000: 1.6 s (15.2× the eagle graph time). Fastest in 0 of 12 cells.
arms.torch_masked: The same array code in PyTorch tensors; it fits where the computation sits next to a PyTorch model or needs autograd. On this card: N = 1,000,000, spread S=100: 167 ms (16.1× the eagle graph time); spread S=1000: 1.68 s (17.8× the eagle graph time); uniform S=1000: 1.68 s (16× the eagle graph time). Fastest in 0 of 12 cells.
arms.torch_graphed: The same PyTorch code with its launch overhead removed by hand: 16 steps captured as one CUDA graph and replayed, one host check per replay, the masking unchanged. On this card: N = 1,000,000, spread S=100: 186 ms (18× the eagle graph time); spread S=1000: 1.68 s (17.8× the eagle graph time); uniform S=1000: 1.68 s (16× the eagle graph time). Fastest in 0 of 12 cells.
arms.torch_compiled: The PyTorch step under torch.compile(mode="reduce-overhead"): Inductor-fused kernels replayed as a CUDA graph. On this card: N = 1,000,000, spread S=100: 25.6 ms (2.48× the eagle graph time); spread S=1000: 251 ms (2.66× the eagle graph time); uniform S=1000: 251 ms (2.38× the eagle graph time). Fastest in 0 of 12 cells.
arms.jax_vmap: The whole loop compiled once, a per-sample while loop batched with vmap; the same code runs on CPUs and GPUs and differentiates with jax.grad. On this card: N = 1,000,000, spread S=100: 25 ms (2.42× the eagle graph time); spread S=1000: 243 ms (2.57× the eagle graph time); uniform S=1000: 242 ms (2.3× the eagle graph time). Fastest in 0 of 12 cells.
arms.warp_kernel: Explicit per-thread kernels written in Python, maintained by NVIDIA and differentiable through wp.Tape; each thread runs its own sample and stops at its own step, so finished samples cost nothing. On this card: N = 1,000,000, spread S=100: 10.7 ms (1.04× the eagle graph time); spread S=1000: 105 ms (1.11× the eagle graph time); uniform S=1000: 119 ms (1.13× the eagle graph time). Fastest in 0 of 12 cells.
arms.cpu_openmp: The same hawk kernel on the host through eagle's OpenMP team, for machines without a GPU. On this card: N = 1,000,000, spread S=100: 33 ms (3.2× the eagle graph time); spread S=1000: 310 ms (3.29× the eagle graph time); uniform S=1000: 352 ms (3.35× the eagle graph time). Fastest in 0 of 12 cells.
